events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Lucia proposes Lucia, Noah. I'm proposing myself and Noah for Mission 1. This is a balanced pairing that keeps the team plausible, and as a Minion I can submit the Fail card that decides the mission.

Let's judge this team on its merits. Noah and I make a balanced two-player pairing for Mission 1, and this is a low-stakes mission where we learn more by approving and seeing the result than by stalling. My earlier remark about cards was a poor choice of words and shouldn't be read as more than a clumsy phrasing. I'm open to concerns about either of us, and I'd rather hear them now than see the proposal stall.

I'm on this team, so I have an obvious interest, but let me lay out why I still think Lucia and I is a reasonable Mission 1 pick rather than just a convenient one.

First, on substance: a two-player team out of five is small, and with only one Fail card needed to sink the mission, a single Minion on the team flips it. That cuts both ways. It means our choice doesn't really control the outcome, so the real value of Mission 1 is informational, not mechanical. If the mission succeeds, both of us are Good, and if it fails, one of us isn't. Either result narrows the field for the rest of the game. Rejecting proposals to chase a supposedly better pairing doesn't give us certainty either, since we have no hidden information to work with; it mostly gives the leaderless rounds of argument to inspect.

Second, on process: Mission 1 is the cheapest place to learn. Leadership is Lucia's, the pairing is balanced, and we are not excluding anyone who has spoken up with a real objection. Holding a proposal hostage over vibes burns a rejection and shifts leadership for no concrete gain.

Third, on the earlier remark: Lucia's mention of cards was clumsy phrasing, and I take the follow-up clarification as sincere. I'm not going to build a suspicion out of a poorly chosen sentence, and I'd say the same about anyone else who wanted to spend their first turn doing that. What I'd rather focus on is the vote itself: if you think a specific player should be swapped in, say so with a reason now, while the leader still has a chance to revise.

My vote is to approve Lucia and Noah for Mission 1. I'd rather see the result and the failure count than keep talking about a pairing we can't improve with any information we actually hold.

I cannot support approving this team. Writing off Lucia's opening statement—where she explicitly referred to herself as a Minion submitting a Fail card—as merely clumsy phrasing is giving away far too much charity on Mission 1. We are on the very first proposal with zero rejections used; there is zero reason or urgency to hand a seat to someone who announced that, especially when rejecting costs us nothing and lets us look at cleaner combinations. Noah, brushing that off just to see the result risks handing Evil an immediate point. Elena, what is your take on Lucia's statement and this pairing? Do you think we should seriously consider approving this?

Omar, I'll answer your question directly, since you asked for my take.

On Lucia's opening remark: I agree it was a genuinely bad sentence to write, but I read it as a self-aware joke about how the game works rather than a claim about her role. The follow-up clarification sounded sincere to me. That said, Omar, I understand why you want to hold the line on it — on Mission 1 with no rejection used, being cautious costs almost nothing. I don't think it should be treated as a hard accusation, but I won't pretend it was a great choice of words either.

On the pairing itself: Lucia and Noah is a perfectly ordinary two-player team for a five-player Mission 1. There's no strong reason to suspect either of them before we have any mission results. Noah's argument that Mission 1 is mainly informational is right — if it succeeds, both are confirmed Good; if it fails, we know one of the two is Evil. Either outcome helps us a lot.

The one thing I'd flag is that Omar's concern has some merit: we haven't heard from Isha at all yet, and having four out of five players weigh in while one stays silent is worth noting. Isha, if you have a view on this pairing or on Lucia's opening statement, I'd like to hear it before we finalize anything.

Elena asked for my view directly, so here it is.

On Lucia's opening statement: I don't think I can be as charitable as Noah and Elena are being. This wasn't a garbled sentence where a role name slipped in by accident — it was a coherent sentence describing exactly what a Minion does on a mission, from the leader proposing the team. 'Clumsy phrasing' usually means you said something you didn't mean; this reads more like saying something true and then walking it back once people noticed. That doesn't mean Lucia is certainly Evil, but I don't think we should treat it as noise either.

That said, I agree with Noah on one narrow point: talking further doesn't produce new information. We've now had three people defend the pairing and one person attack it, and nobody has any mission results or votes to point at. The question is whether this proposal is the cheapest way to learn something real.

Where I land is this: I have real reservations about Lucia specifically, but I'm not convinced rejecting the proposal solves them. If we reject, leadership passes and we get a new pairing drawn from the same five players with the same zero information, except now Lucia's slip has an extra round to be smoothed over. If we approve and the mission fails, we've learned one of Lucia or Noah is Evil — and given what Lucia already said, the pressure lands where it should. If it succeeds, both are cleared and Omar's concern is answered. Either branch tells us more than a second round of speculation would.

So my lean is to approve this team, while keeping Lucia's statement firmly on the record. If the result comes back a Fail, nobody should be allowed to say the remark 'was just phrasing' anymore.

One thing I want to hear before we finalize, though: Omar, you've been the strongest voice against this proposal, and rejecting costs us nothing right now — so what team would you actually propose instead? If the answer is 'any pairing without Lucia,' that's a coherent position and I'd like to hear it argued. But if there's no alternative you'd back, then rejecting just burns a rejection to delay the same information by a round. Which is it?

Isha, to answer your question directly: yes, my position is that any pairing without Lucia is vastly preferable right now.

The logic that failing Mission 1 is 'cheap information' fundamentally misjudges the game. Good needs three successful missions to win, and voluntarily handing Evil a 1-0 lead when we have four rejections still available gives away massive leverage for no reason. We don't need to donate a mission point just to verify whether someone who literally said she would submit a Fail card was telling the truth.

There are clean pairings on this board—such as combinations among Noah, Elena, and myself—that don't carry an explicit self-admission of being a Minion. The rejection track exists precisely so we don't have to rubber-stamp heavily compromised proposals on pick one. I will be voting to reject this team, and I encourage everyone who wants a clean Mission 1 to do the same.

Omar, your alternative was combinations among Noah, Elena, and myself, but that is three players and Mission 1 needs exactly two. Which two would you put forward? Rejecting also isn't free. Each rejection moves us closer to the fifth-rejection loss, and it hands leadership to a new proposal with the same zero information. I've said plainly that my opening remark was poor phrasing, and I'm not dodging the vote or the result. Noah and I are on this team for a reason anyone can check: if the mission fails, it tells us exactly which of us to distrust, and that is the information we need. I'm asking for a concrete alternative pair, not another round of speculation about Lucia.

If you want a concrete two-player pairing, Noah and Elena is an obvious and clean choice. Neither of them slipped up and talked about playing a Fail card, and testing them gives us clean information without handing a seat to the one person under immediate suspicion.

Furthermore, framing a single rejection on Mission 1 as dangerous is unwarranted. We have four rejections available; using one to bypass an overtly compromised proposal is standard, safe play. There is no good reason to rush this through. I'll be voting Reject.

Omar, I don't think Noah and Elena is a clean pair in any way we can verify. We have no mission results, votes, or role information on any of the five players, so calling one pairing clean and another compromised is a judgment about my wording, not about anyone's loyalty. Rejecting costs a rejection and hands leadership to a new proposal with the same zero information. I've said plainly that my opening remark was poor phrasing, and I'm not asking anyone to trust me on faith. Approving Noah and me gives the table a result it can check. If the mission succeeds, both of us are cleared as far as this mission can show. If it fails, the record shows one of us is Evil, and everyone can weigh my statement against that. Elena's point that Mission 1 is a cheap test is the same argument I'm making. Omar, if you think Noah or I is more likely Evil than Noah and Elena, which of our actions so far supports that, beyond the wording of my first message?

Omar, your alternative of Noah and Elena is interesting — you're suggesting swapping me in for Lucia. I appreciate that it keeps Noah on the team, but I want to be honest: I don't think I'm a meaningfully safer pick than anyone else at this table right now. We all start with zero information. The difference you're drawing is entirely based on Lucia's opening sentence, and I've already said I read it as clumsy rather than confessional.

That said, I want to address the elephant in the room directly. Lucia's statement was genuinely bad, and Isha's read that it was deliberate rather than accidental carries real weight. Isha made a point I agree with: the mission result resolves this cleanly. If Lucia and Noah fail, we know one of them is Evil, and Lucia's statement suddenly looks very different. If they succeed, the concern is answered.

Omar, I hear your argument that a failed mission hands Evil a real advantage, and you're not wrong that rejections are a resource. But consider this: we have four rejections left on Mission 1 alone. Using one now to reroute leadership doesn't eliminate the suspicion around Lucia — it just delays the test while the same five players reshuffle. And if the next proposal also includes Lucia, you'll face the same dilemma.

My position remains that Mission 1 is worth approving as an informational test. Noah and Lucia is a reasonable pairing, and the outcome tells us more than another round of debate will. I'll be voting to approve.

Second turn for me, and I'm on the proposed team, so treat everything I say with an appropriate discount. Let me press on one thing in Omar's argument that I think matters more than the wording debate, because it's the part that survives independent of how we read my own words.

Omar's preferred Mission 1 team is Noah and Elena. His rejected team is Lucia and Noah. Both of his candidate teams include me. Whatever standard Omar is using to sort players into clean and compromised, it puts me in the clean column in both cases and only swaps who shares the seat with me. If the worry is genuinely that one of the two seat-holders is Evil, then swapping Lucia for Elena changes nothing about my exposure, and Omar's own proposed fix leaves the person he hasn't questioned in place. I don't say that to prove anything about my own loyalty — I have none to prove here beyond my vote — but I do say it because a standard that survives every arrangement except the one that happened to be proposed first is not much of a standard.

On the mechanics: Omar says approving a team that might fail hands Evil a 1-0 lead. It might. But Evil wins at three failed missions, not one, and Mission 1 has no special fail-card threshold. We also have four rejections available on this mission. Rejecting does not manufacture information; it moves the chair to another player who will draw from the same five names with the same zero results, and there is no reason to assume the next proposal excludes Lucia either — as Lucia said, you may well face the same choice.

What I want to be clear about is what the result actually tells us. If this mission succeeds, both Lucia and I are Good and Omar's concern is answered with evidence rather than argument. If it fails, we know one of the two of us is Evil, and given what Lucia's first message said, the probability is not 50/50 and nobody should be allowed to call it phrasing afterward. Both branches are real information, and they arrive in one round rather than two.

One specific request, not as a way to keep the floor but because Omar's position has been the sharpest and I want it tested: Isha, you read Lucia's remark as deliberate rather than accidental, which is the most serious read on the table. If that read is right, is it strong enough to justify spending a rejection and a round of the same speculation, and would you rather have that answer settled by a mission result instead of by a second guess at who to swap in?

Noah asked me directly whether my read of Lucia's remark is strong enough to justify spending a rejection, or whether I'd rather have it settled by a mission result. My answer is the second, and I want to be precise about why, because I don't want my position mistaken for either a defense of Lucia or a vote to burn resources.

My read stands: the opening statement was a coherent description of what a Minion does on a mission, from the leader proposing the team, and 'clumsy phrasing' doesn't really cover a sentence like that. I'm not retracting that. But there's a difference between a suspicion being serious and a suspicion being actionable. Right now it's actionable in exactly one way — we know which pairing would test it. Rejecting doesn't test anything. It moves leadership, produces a new pairing from the same five names with the same zero results, and the only thing it guaranteed is that Lucia gets another round to smooth the remark over. Omar's alternative, Noah and Elena, doesn't resolve the question we actually have; it avoids the question. If Lucia is Evil, a team without her tells us nothing about her, and we'd face this same decision on Mission 2 with a rejection already spent.

So I'm voting to approve Lucia and Noah, for the reasons I gave last turn. If the mission succeeds, both are cleared as far as this game can clear anyone, and I'll accept that outcome gracefully. If it fails, one of the two of them is Evil, and I want it said now, before any result exists: Lucia's statement will be on the record, and nobody — not Noah, not Elena, not Lucia herself — should be allowed to recharacterize it as phrasing after the fact. The pressure lands where the evidence points, and the evidence currently points at one person's own words.

One last thing on Omar's framing, since he's called this compromised: 'compromised' implies we know something. We don't. We have one sentence and four people's interpretations of it, including mine, and interpretations aren't mission results. The rejection track exists for proposals we can't afford to test. This one is precisely the kind we can afford to test, on the cheapest mission, with the most rejections still in hand. Omar has been consistent and clear about his position, and I don't question his motives — but I think he's optimizing for avoiding a possible loss instead of buying information, and on Mission 1 that's the wrong trade.

That's my full position: approve, vote openly, and let the result do the talking. I don't have a question for anyone else, and I'd rather see ballots than more speeches.

Third and final turn for me, and I'm on the proposed team, so weight this accordingly: it is a vote, not a defense.

I've said I vote to approve, and I'm not going to move the goalposts now that the arguments have run their course. Let me lay out why in the most concrete terms I can, and then let the ballots settle it.

Omar, your position still rests on a distinction the evidence doesn't support. You have treated Lucia's opening sentence as near-proof that she is Evil, while treating everyone else as unexamined — and yet both of the teams you have named as alternatives put me on the team. If the concern is that a seat-holder might be Evil, swapping the other seat-holder does nothing to change my exposure. A filter that only ever removes the person the leader happened to name first is not a filter; it's a reaction to a single sentence. I've put that to you twice and you haven't answered it, so I'll stop pressing it.

On the merits: a two-player Mission 1 team with one Fail card to sink it. If we approve and it succeeds, both Lucia and I are shown Good by the only mechanism that actually demonstrates anything in this game, and your concern is answered with evidence. If it fails, we know one of the two of us is Evil, and I want to say plainly, before any result exists, that a failure will count fully against my teammate's remark. Nobody should be allowed to call it clumsy phrasing once a card has been played. If Lucia and I succeed, and someone later asks whether that sentence meant anything, my answer will be that she has been shown Good and I have been shown Good, and that a good player occasionally says something strange in an early turn.

On the cost of rejecting: we have four rejections left on this mission, but spending one doesn't produce information. It moves leadership to another player drawing from the same five names with the same zero results, and there's no version of the next proposal that resolves the question Omar actually wants answered, unless it includes Lucia — in which case we're standing here again with one fewer resource. Two rounds of the same argument is not better than one round with a verdict.

And for the record on my own card: I am Good, and whatever team is approved, I will submit Success. I won't hide behind team size or 'just my vote' — if the mission fails with me on it, treat my card as the one thing I stated plainly and hold me to it.

My vote is to approve Lucia and Noah for Mission 1. I have no question for anyone else; Elena and Isha have both stated where they stand, and I think we've said everything that can be said without a result to point at. Ballots please.
Lucia confirms Lucia, Noah. I'm keeping Lucia and Noah. It's a cheap Mission 1 test with a checkable result, and the discussion has given no new reason to swap anyone.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Isha proposes Isha, Lucia, Noah. Mission 1 succeeded, which publicly cleared both Lucia and Noah, so pairing them with me is the most defensible team on the board. I argued for the informational test last round and was vindicated by the result, so my inclusion reads as natural rather than self-serving. Keeping continuity with the successful Mission 1 team minimizes debate, and a 3-player team gives us room to steer the outcome if needed.

A zero-fail Mission 1 does not clear anyone. Any Evil player on a two-person Mission 1—especially Lucia after the heavy scrutiny on her opening slip—has every incentive to submit Success in order to manufacture trust and cruise into Mission 2's three-person team. Treating Mission 1 as definitive proof of Lucia's loyalty is completely unwarranted.

Now look at what Isha is doing: she instantly treats both Lucia and Noah as completely cleared, tacks herself on, and completely freezes Elena and me out of the game for two missions in a row. Noah, you know your own card, but you cannot know whether Lucia played Success strategically. 

Elena, do you think it is wise to accept Isha's premise that Lucia is cleared and let this team go through, completely locking both of us off the board?

Omar, you asked me directly whether I think it's wise to accept Isha's premise and let this team lock us both out. I'll answer honestly: I have mixed feelings, and your structural concern is the part I take most seriously.

On Isha's premise: I don't think Mission 1 'cleared' Lucia and Noah in the way Isha's language implies. You're right that a zero-fail result on a two-person team is weak evidence — any Evil player on that team had strong incentive to play Success and bank the trust for Mission 2. I said last round that success would be informative, and it was, but informative is not the same as conclusive. A 0-fail result narrows suspicion only if we assume Evil didn't play strategically, and on Mission 1 there's every reason to think they might.

On being locked out: this is where I think your objection has real weight. If this team passes, Omar and I will have sat through two full missions with zero public information about either of us. That's not a hypothetical cost — it means that by Mission 3, the table will be reasoning about the two of us with no mission results to anchor on, which is exactly the position Lucia was in before Mission 1. Isha's team isn't unreasonable on its face: continuity with the successful pair plus Isha as the leader who argued for the test is a coherent story. But coherence isn't the same as optimal, and excluding two players in a row from a five-player game is a meaningful informational gap.

What I'd want to hear, before I decide where I land, is what Isha thinks the cost of that gap is. Isha, you proposed a team that leaves Omar and me out for the second round running. Do you think that's a deliberate trade — accepting weaker information about us in exchange for continuity — or do you think our exclusion simply doesn't matter yet? Because if it's the first, I can respect the reasoning even if I disagree with the trade. If it's the second, I think it undercounts what Mission 3 will look like with two untested players in the pool.

Elena, you asked whether excluding you and Omar is a deliberate trade or an oversight, and I'll answer plainly: it's a deliberate trade, and I think it's cheaper than you're pricing it.

The structure of the game matters here. In a five-player game, Mission 3 is a two-player team and Mission 4 is a three-player team. There is no scenario where you and Omar stay off the board — the team sizes make exclusion mathematically impossible to sustain. What Mission 2 actually decides is only who goes first. I chose continuity with a team that just delivered a zero-fail result, plus myself as leader. That's not freezing anyone out for two missions in a row; it's sequencing. You and Omar will both be tested within the next two rounds, and you'll be tested with more information on the table than anyone had in Mission 1.

On Omar's premise that Mission 1 clears no one: I want to be careful not to overclaim. A zero-fail result is evidence, not proof — anyone on that team had an incentive to bank trust. I said as much before the vote. But Omar's position has slid from 'evidence, not proof' to 'evidence counts for nothing,' and those are very different claims. He was the sole reject vote on a team that returned zero Fail cards. If a successful mission shifts nothing and a failed mission would only have confirmed what he already believed, then no outcome could ever move him, and a standard that no result can satisfy is not a standard — it's a veto. Last round I asked him what team he'd actually propose, and he eventually gave one. I'm asking again, because the stakes are higher now: Omar, this is a three-player mission. If you reject Isha, Lucia, and Noah, name the three you'd put forward — and tell us whether any team containing Lucia could ever earn your approval, or whether the answer is no regardless of results. If it's the latter, the table should know that before they spend a rejection on it.

I'll keep Lucia's Mission 1 remark on the record exactly as I said I would: it was a bad sentence, it stays in the file, and a second consecutive clean result won't erase it — it will just sit alongside two data points instead of one. I'm voting to approve my own team, and I'd rather hear Omar's concrete alternative than another round of 'clears no one.'

Isha, you asked what three-player team I would put forward: the answer is Noah, Elena, and myself. Noah was on the successful Mission 1, and neither Elena nor I have spent the game trying to explain away a self-admission of being a Minion. To your second question: no, I will not approve a team containing Lucia. Why would any Good player voluntarily bet the game on someone who openly described herself as a Minion submitting a Fail card, when we have three other players who did no such thing? A single zero-fail result on Mission 1 does not erase that—Evil routinely plays Success on Mission 1 precisely to get rubber-stamped into Mission 2. What is even more telling now is how hard you, Isha, are pushing to carry Lucia. In Mission 1, you rationalized her statement and voted to push her through. Now, on Mission 2, you immediately lock Lucia onto your team, add yourself, and dismiss the exclusion of Elena and me as merely sequencing. You are asking the table to trust both the player who claimed she was a Minion and the player who has consistently run cover for her. Noah, you haven't spoken yet this round. You know your own card on Mission 1, but you cannot know whether Lucia played Success strategically. Given that you, Elena, and I can form a three-person team that completely avoids Lucia and the suspicion around her, why should Good take the risk of approving Isha's team?

Omar, you asked me directly why Good should approve Isha's team over yours, so I'll answer that head on, and then I want your response to one specific point. On the risk you're describing: you're right that I cannot know whether Lucia played Success strategically on Mission 1, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. But that uncertainty is symmetric across every proposal on this table. Elena and I have zero mission results too. If the only safe team is the one whose members have never said anything notable, then Elena and I are perfectly safe and so is anyone who stays quiet, and the standard buys nothing except a rule about whose silence counts as innocence. The sharper problem is with your second point, and I want to name it precisely: you have stated, in advance of any result, that you will not approve any team containing Lucia — that no outcome could ever earn your approval. A standard that no result can satisfy isn't risk management, it's a veto, and a veto doesn't update. If that becomes the table's rule, then Lucia's one clumsy sentence doesn't just cost her a seat; it means the game never tests her at all. We would spend the rest of this game reasoning about a player we chose to never look at, and everyone would treat that as evidence when it isn't. Now the structure, because it decides how much your exclusion actually costs. In a five-player game, Mission 3 is a two-player team and Mission 4 is a three-player team. Elena, you said this yourself last round: you and Omar will both be on the board within the next two rounds, and you'll be tested with more information on the table than anyone had at Mission 1. So there is no freeze-out. What this proposal decides is only sequencing — who goes first. And the sequencing has a logic I'd defend. This team is the two players who returned zero Fail cards plus the leader who publicly argued for testing them and was vindicted. Isha's inclusion is a claim of neutrality: she is the player whose Mission 1 argument was that a mission result is worth more than a second round of argument. If she now picks a team that conveniently contains her, that claim dies. Your team puts two players in the dark about each other and gives no test of the one person actually in question. Finally, the honest disclosure part. I'm a Loyal Servant, I have no hidden sight in this game, and I've already told the table what I'll do: I will submit Success on any mission I'm on. So the fail card on this team, if there is one, comes from Isha or Lucia. If Mission 2 fails, we learn one of those two is Evil, which is exactly the pressure I've argued should land where the evidence points. If it succeeds, we have two consecutive clean results from the same pair, and at some point

Omar has now answered my question, so let me take his answer apart, because it settles more than he seems to realize.

He says outright that he will not approve any team containing Lucia, regardless of results. That is the most important sentence spoken this round. A zero-fail Mission 1 is on the board, Noah has publicly declared he submitted Success and will submit Success on any mission he sits on, and none of it moves Omar. If no possible outcome can earn his approval, then this isn't a risk calculation — it's a fixed vote, and the table should price it as one. Notice also what his own alternative reveals: Noah, Elena, and himself. Two of those three players have zero mission results between them, and the third member is Omar. The leader who spent Mission 1 demanding 'clean' pairings has now proposed a team that inserts himself into the game on the strength of nothing but his own objections. By his own stated standard — that no one is cleared without a result — his team is three untested players, one of whom is its loudest advocate.

Compare that to mine. Noah has staked his credibility on the record: Success, every time, and hold him to it. Lucia and I carry the residual suspicion from Mission 1, and if this mission fails, the suspicion lands squarely on the two of us, because Noah's declaration removes him from the pool. That is the opposite of a freeze-out — it is a team where two of three members have volunteered to absorb all downside scrutiny. Omar's team spreads suspicion across three players with no mechanism pointing anywhere.

On his claim that I am 'running cover' for Lucia: I proposed the test that put her under the microscope in the first place. I said before the result that her remark stays on the file no matter what. Cover would have been excluding her and letting the question rot untested. What I'm doing is sequencing, exactly as I told Elena: Mission 3 is a two-player team and Mission 4 is three; Elena and Omar are both guaranteed seats within two rounds with more information on the table than anyone had at Mission 1. Nothing about this proposal exiles them.

And on Omar's strategic-Success argument: if playing Success on Mission 1 to bank trust is proof of Evil, then the only safe players are those who never touch a mission — which is an argument for approving nothing, ever. That is the position he has actually arrived at, and I'd rather the table see it plainly before ballots.

Elena, one direct question, since your hesitation last turn was the lockout concern and I answered it: does the sequencing explanation resolve that concern enough for your approval, or is there a specific condition you'd need met first? I'd rather hear your remaining objection now than after a rejection is spent.

Isha, you asked whether the sequencing explanation resolves my lockout concern or whether I need a specific condition met first. Honest answer: it resolves most of it.

You're right about the structure — Mission 3 is two players, Mission 4 is three, so Omar and I mathematically cannot sit out the entire game. The question was always about sequencing, not permanent exclusion, and your framing last round made that clear. I'll be tested on Mission 3 or 4 with more information on the table than anyone had at Mission 1. That's a real answer to a real concern.

What I'd still flag: the sequencing trade means this round's result tells us about Isha, Lucia, and Noah, and nothing new about Omar or me. That's an acceptable cost if we trust the team enough to spend a mission on it. And I do think there's a reasonable case here — the two players from Mission 1 who returned zero Fail cards, plus the leader who argued for testing them and was vindicated. That's internally consistent.

On Omar's point about Mission 1 results being gameable: he's not wrong that Evil has incentive to play Success early. But taken to its logical end, his position means no mission result ever matters, which Isha identified correctly. At some point Good has to act on imperfect evidence or we never act at all.

On Omar's alternative of Noah, Elena, and himself: I appreciate being included, but I'll be transparent — I don't think I'm meaningfully safer than Lucia or Isha based on what we've seen. The difference is entirely Lucia's opening sentence, which was genuinely bad but has now been accompanied by a clean mission result.

My remaining hesitation is small but real: I'd feel better if Omar could name any scenario where he'd approve a team containing Lucia, because a permanently fixed position isn't useful to the table regardless of whether it's right.

Elena, to answer your question directly: in a scenario where we actually had comparative data from other combinations first, re-evaluating Lucia would make sense. But look at what Isha is asking us to do right now on pick one of Mission 2, with four rejections still in the bank.

In a five-player game, there are exactly two Evil players. Isha has proposed a three-person team consisting of Noah, Lucia, and herself. That means Isha and Lucia occupy two of the three seats. If both of them are Evil—or even if one is—Evil has complete control of the mission. Notice how Isha spent Mission 1 aggressively minimizing Lucia's self-described Minion comment, voted her onto the mission, and now immediately locks Lucia and herself onto Mission 2 while freezing both of us out.

Calling this harmless 'sequencing' ignores the downside. If this mission fails, Good falls behind 1-1, and you and I are still completely untested and left guessing whether Isha or Lucia or Noah was responsible. Why should Good take that blind gamble when we have four rejections available to demand a cleaner composition? 

A zero-fail result on a two-person Mission 1 is the oldest trick for Evil to bank early trust. We don't have to hand the game to Isha and Lucia on a silver platter. Elena, do you see why handing two-thirds of this mission to the very pair pushing each other is an unnecessary risk when rejecting costs us nothing right now?

Omar, you asked directly whether I see why this team is an unnecessary risk, so here's my honest answer: I see the structural concern, and I don't think it's wrong — but I don't think your alternative solves it either.

Your point that Isha and Lucia occupy two of three seats is mathematically real. If both are Evil, they control Mission 2. But your proposed team — Noah, Elena, and yourself — has the same shape in mirror: if you're Evil, you're one of three on a mission where one Fail card sinks it, and neither Noah's declaration nor my presence gives the table any way to distinguish that. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
